utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Good morning. Could we have the case called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is IT-04-83-PT, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the representation for the parties. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Kyle Wood, Ruth Frolich, and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to my learned friends from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mrs. Quincy Whitaker, I appear on behalf of General Rasim Delic. Together with us is our case manager Ms. Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we go into the subject matter, let me first offer my apologies for we not being able to hold the traditional 65 ter conference. As you know, the reason for that was a change of guard in the Senior Legal Officer's position, but I know that the parties met yesterday and before that there was also an exchange of letters which I'm privy to. So I'm certain that we, as far as preparations are concerned, are ready to go. Before we enter into, for what the parties may seem to be outstanding matters, let me just go through what I think we have before us as far as pending motions. We have a motion regarding judicial notice of adjudicated facts, which was timely submitted by the Prosecution. We have a response containing a request for a stay, which was granted by the -- by the Chamber, and that was due to the non-translation of the Hadzihasanovic case into English. And the ruling is that once that is completed, the re-filing shall be made in two days and then the Defence has 14 days to respond to that. I believe now that the translation is imminent in the sense that it will probably be completed before the end of this month. So we expect to have these things complied with according to the order. We also have the submission of agreed facts by the Prosecution filed on the 18th of October, 2006, so we'll come back to the question of agreed facts later. The third motion is a motion filed the day before yesterday from the Prosecution regarding protective measures and delayed disclosure. That was a re-filing following a decision on the 8th of November because the original motion was ex parte and it was felt it should be interparties. And I can assure you that the Chamber would deal with that motion as soon as it's ready. It's pending a reply from the Defence. So those were the motions that, from this side, are pending at the moment. By nods, I see that we are in agreement on this. Could we then move to the question of outstanding issues which were reflected in the exchange of letters that I saw. As I said, you had a meeting, my understanding, yesterday, and I hope that that was satisfactory in the sense that you managed to solve, if not all, at least most of the matters. It dealt with disclosure matters and it was from the Defence a lot of clarifications and answers were sought. So I turn to Defence first. I ask whether you are now satisfied or whether you have any outstanding matters relating to that exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will start with Rule 66(A)(i), that is the obligation on the part of the Prosecutor to disclose evidence according to that Rule. What was missing was a statement. We went through the material forwarded yesterday by the OTP. We received 27 CDs, and to the extent we were able to go through it, I believe we now have that material in our possession. Although I must say here that we haven't been able to go through all of it and we weren't able to verify whether we received all the material put by the OTP to various witnesses as regards footage and documents. Therefore, we will address the OTP. We will send a letter as regards that. As for 66(A)(ii), we discussed this at length yesterday with the OTP, and yesterday they turned over 22 DVDs and you will understand of course that we will -- were unable to check them all. We just went through it quickly, and we established that there are six statements missing. As for the Prosecutor, they told us that there were five missing; however, after this session, we will meet the OTP yet again, upon their request, and we'll try to settle that matter. Of course, we also expect the OTP to turn over all the material shown to various witnesses, be it the witnesses whose statements we have from before. And the OTP claimed yesterday that we were given all that, although I cannot verify that necessarily today. However, we also wish to receive all the material shown to witnesses, the video material, photographs, documents, and so on and so forth, on top of the six statements. There is a difference in position between us and the Prosecutor when it comes to these statements. The Prosecutor mentioned five; we mentioned six. It seems to me that the Prosecutor believes that they are not duty-bound at this moment to forward those statements because not all the statements have been taken from all the witnesses. But I believe that falls under 66(A)(ii) as well; namely, these are witnesses that the Prosecutor intends to call here. Therefore, we need to have all the material shown to them so as to be able to respond and to prepare our case. We need to be able to put together our pre-trial brief. That's why I do not believe that that material falls under the category of other witnesses. Something else that was discussed yesterday, and I wanted to have that in the transcript of this Status Conference. And it is the following: We received a letter on the 29th of September which concerned disclosure according to 66(A)(ii), in which the OTP stressed that until the 31st of October, as directed by the Chamber, will forward a list to the Defence. In that letter, the OTP states that they are to forward an interim list, a provisional one, and they stated that it is their right to add other witnesses to the list in the period before the commencement of the trial. This will, of course, be regulated by the Chamber's decision or decisions. This is my third case before this Tribunal, and I have some unfortunate experience with such OTP policies; namely, I just wouldn't like to see things from the Oric case happen again. We were there -- put in a situation in which we received one list concerning 66(A)(ii), and then a few months or six months later, immediately prior to the commencement of the trial, the list is changed so as to remove 20 witnesses and add another large group of, say, 12. I believe this is not something that falls under the Rules. Actually, I believe that is contrary to Rule 21, item 4(b) of the Statute, if I recollect it accurately. We need the time and the means to prepare the case. In such a case, if we are given 12 new witnesses immediately prior to the trial, we cannot prepare ourselves for a quality cross-examination. We just wanted to state this in advance. I'm not stating it is going to take place; I just wanted to have this in the record, however. Another thing concerning 66(A)(ii). The Prosecutor submitted their motion as regards delayed disclosure for protected witnesses; however, I believe that they should have included a summary in their pre-trial brief, the summary of what that witness is to testify about, that is the witness's code and the summary of evidence. We have the right to prepare and to know what it will concern generally speaking. Yesterday we were told by the Prosecutor, that's at least the way I understood it, that their brief will contain a redacted statement. I hope we will see it as soon as possible, since we haven't received it up until now. I believe I said enough as regards 66(A)(ii) for the time being, but while I'm still on my feet, perhaps I can address Rule 92 bis as well. We haven't received that material, and the OTP confirmed that they are not to disclose this moment and that no brief will be submitted. As regards 94 bis, the Prosecutor confirmed that they agree with us on the deadline of 30 days in which we, as the other party, are to provide a reply concerning the expert findings, but that deadline has not been set in motion. In our view, statements are incomplete, there are parts missing, based on which we could assess the expert's knowledge and competence. In any case, I want to state here that we will ask for cross-examination of all proposed witnesses, provided the Prosecutor forwards their statements according to 92 bis. We will also object to parts of witness statements as regards their competence to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic. Comments from you, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a couple of quick comments, particularly with respect to Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure. It is, in fact, the case that with respect to five of the witnesses listed on the Prosecution's witness list that was filed on the 31st of October, 2006, that the Prosecution does not have written witness statements with respect to those five witnesses. There is, in our respectful submission, no requirement for written witness statements, although, of course, if we have them, we disclose them. Having said that, we anticipate in the very near future, within the next two to three months, taking written witness statements from several of those five individuals. It would seem, although, again, without having the benefit of having the Defence provided enough time to go through the materials that were disclosed to them, I would venture to say that the sixth missing statement that Mrs. Vidovic refers to probably relates to the witness who is the subject of the delayed disclosure motion. And again, pending a ruling from the Trial Chamber, we would provide a redacted version of that statement as soon as we were ordered to do so by the Trial Chamber. With respect to the materials shown to the witnesses, I believe with a couple of exceptions - and those were indicated in previous correspondence - that all such materials have been provided to the Defence. Of course, our position is very clear on this and let me make it absolutely clear. If a document or a photograph or a video or a map was shown to a witness during the course of their interview, and that is referred to in the witness's written statement, we will disclose that document, photograph, video, or map to the Defence. It's sometimes a question of missing material when we review the statements and don't necessarily capture all of the material. Sometimes documents are referred to in witness statements by date or by a brief description of the document, but the document in question does not yet -- at that time, did not have an ERN number. So some of these materials, just as would be the case for the Defence, are sometimes difficult for us to then locate five or six years later based on a brief description in a statement. In the event the Defence is missing any of that material, still missing any of that material, with the exception of the two or three items I specifically indicated will be forthcoming, clearly, we will provide that material as soon as they can identify to us specifically what is missing. With respect to adding witnesses and exhibits, clearly, we are in the Trial Chamber's hands in that respect. We filed our witness list, we filed our exhibit list. I believe Ms. Vidovic was referring to a footnote in the cover motion to our pre-trial brief, whereby we specifically reserve the right to seek leave, to either file a revised pre-trial brief shortly before -- by shortly before, I don't mean two weeks, I mean several months before trial. We may seek leave to file an updated pre-trial brief. We, of course, are fully aware that to add or to alter the witness list or to add to or to alter the exhibit list requires the leave of the Trial Chamber. And make no mistakes about that. We are not going to be unilaterally making any changes to either of those documents. We would be doing so only after having sought leave of the Trial Chamber and being granted such leave. And finally, with respect to the witness that was the subject of the delayed disclosure motion that was filed on the 13th of November, I believe that we have provided in that motion an adequate summary of the expected testimony of that witness for the benefit of the Defence, but again, we will be in a position to provide a redacted version of that witness's written statement as soon as we are ordered to do so by the Trial Chamber. Turning very quickly to Rule 92 bis clearly -- what we've indicated in our 65 ter filing is what the Rule requires, an indication of which witnesses we anticipate might be 92 bis witnesses. We, at this point, of course, are not filing a motion seeking that those 92 bis statements be admitted into evidence. It is, based on my experience here and the jurisprudence, it's a bit premature to be making such a filing for the actual admission of 92 bis statements. So that, of course, is an issue for the future. Similarly, with respect to the 94 bis expert reports that have been disclosed, I informed the Defence yesterday that it was not our interpretation of the Rule necessarily that -- that they have now 30 days to respond to those expert reports, but simply -- I believe that the Rule basically requires them to inform us whether they accept the statement and whether they want to cross-examine the witnesses, and I believe Mrs. Vidovic has done that. In our respectful view, the Defence [sic], at this point in time, is not required to make any further submissions concerning those expert reports. It's entirely up to the Defence whether they wish to do that now or at a later point in time. I believe those are all the subjects that Mrs. Vidovic has raised thus far. So let me just sit down at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, we have one overriding uncertainty, that is that Ms. Vidovic has not been able to absorb the material that was handed over to her yesterday. So one could anticipate that out of that could come yet other unclear matters. But let me clarify one thing, and that relates to the necessity to give Mrs. Vidovic and the Defence a redacted version of the -- of the statement relating to the motion of the protective measures and delayed disclosure. You are hereby so ordered to do that and do that -- what is practical for you that would seem not many days, but give me an indication when you can have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The interview of that witness, Your Honour, was tape recorded and took place over the course of approximately three days. So it's not a five- or eight-page written single-spaced statement, it is rather a transcript that runs many, many pages, probably several hundred pages. I don't expect it would take us a significant period of time to do that, but I will notify the Defence and perhaps the Trial Chamber by way of letter to -- via the Legal Officer, as to an expected date when we would be in a position to do that. I would not anticipate that it would take us longer than a week, but it would be difficult for me to commit to that standing here right now. But it should be a matter of just a few days I would think, perhaps a week. But I will consult with the actual person who was involved in the interview, who obviously is the best-placed person to do that, to make those redactions, and get an indication from him as to how long that might take and inform the Defence and the Trial Chamber via the Legal Officer accordingly, if that's satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. I think we should nail it down to a week from today, and then obviously the response time for the Defence is computed from the end of that submission. Regarding the question of 94 bis, I think it's also proper, despite the generosity shown by you, Mr. Mundis, to also clarify that when it comes to the time in which you should react, and you have reacted today Mrs. Vidovic, indicating your wish to cross-examine, is that the 30-day period should run as of today or when some outstanding issues connected to that has been handed over to you in B/C/S. So either 30 days from today or 30 days from when you have received the full material in B/C/S from the Prosecution related to the expert reports. Let me offer also a comment on the question of the change of witness and evidence. There were, obviously, two filings in the sense -- the 29th of September and also the pre-trial brief. I also, Mr. Mundis, noticed the footnote which Mrs. Vidovic already has, through you, indicated that she has, namely, that there seems to be, from your side, an opinion that if the case is not docketed, the pre-trial brief could be compiled with a lighter touch. Let me call it the pre-trial brief light, than if the case is docketed. That is not the opinion of the Chamber, and for very good reasons. Even if the global scheduling and docketing of cases is not within our hands, it's our duty to make sure that this case is brought forward. And for, again, the very simple reason: If the best-laid plans are not fulfilled, the Court would perhaps find itself in a position where there would be room available but no cases ready. So I think the notion of not taking the pre-trial brief seriously -- I'm not saying, Mr. Mundis, that you haven't, but the footnote that you indicated is sort of -- was something that I think should be brought to the fore in this matter and also to encourage you, obviously, Mrs. Vidovic, to make sure that the Defence brief is written in the light of this is the brief, as it were. Any comments? I think this is fully clear. By nods, I see that you are in agreement. Let me offer, regarding any other outstanding issues that we have touched upon here now, the possibility that we -- if the parties are unable to solve the outstanding issues between yourselves, the court officers or the Senior Legal Officer who could then arrange a meeting, and you could sort out the outstanding issues. I'm thinking of the question of supporting materials and others. I think those things could be cleared, and as I said, other matters will possibly need to be raised once you have absorbed the material you received yesterday. I don't think we need to set a time for that meeting. It could either be before you are to file your Defence brief, Mrs. Vidovic, or it could be immediately thereafter. We will work through the Senior Legal Officer to make sure that this is set up. Would that be to the parties' liking?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's completely satisfactory to the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we then, for completeness, should just comment on some of the issues we haven't touched upon. We noticed at the last Status Conference in the end of June that the Defence did not intend to offer any special defence. The time-limit for offering that has now expired and I take it the position is unchanged, Mrs. Vidovic. By your nod, I see that you agree. We have also received, as indicated, the agreed facts from the Prosecution. We have the outstanding issue of adjudicated facts. But I would like to encourage -- and I think that was anticipated in the Prosecution's submission on agreed facts that there will be additions to it. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: One always tries to remain optimistic and hopeful in such situations. Certainly, additional agreed facts are something that the Prosecution takes very seriously and I know the Defence do as well. One of the issues for the agenda between the parties commencing at 9.30 this morning will be perhaps some -- setting some time-lines or at least exchanging views on additional agreed facts. I assure you that we will continue working together in that regard with respect to coming up with some additional agreed facts and narrowing the issues that will be litigated at trial to the bare minimum number of issues. I'm extremely hopeful that we will be able to do that in the spirit of cooperation with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. And, Mrs. Vidovic, your testimony to this effect?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to raise another issue today concerning pre-trial briefs, and I believe there may be problems with it during the trial itself; namely, the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief contains Annex C. It is a list of 52 victims killed in Vozica. When we received the indictment, we objected to its imprecision concerning that. It contained a small number of names. At a certain point, the Prosecutor added the names of 52 people, as it seems. However, Your Honour, if you look at the names in Annex C, you will notice that the degree of its imprecision is such that we are unable to deal with it. We cannot prepare for our case. For example, person number 6 is given two names Cvjetko or Svetko Kaurin born on this or that year in this or that town. For some people, we have two names, two different years of birth, and two different places of birth. Your Honour, this is something which is completely unacceptable for us. We cannot prepare our case against this part of the indictment, provided the annex remains as such. I just wanted to direct your attention to it in a timely fashion. I believe that the Army of Republika Srpska did, indeed, keep neat records on soldiers killed, and I believe this problem should have been overcome by now. What I need to point out is that we will not be able to run any checks whether some of those people have indeed been killed or whether they are alive. We cannot run our checks with two differents names and two different years of birth. And sometimes the years differ by a full decade and sometimes we have even up to three places of birth. I wanted to have this on the record because it presents a problem. Another thing, Your Honour, you were probably able to see it for yourself in the previous Status Conferences' transcripts. I discussed the application of Rule 68 at length and the different interpretations between the two parties. It seems to me that at a certain point we have overcome that problem and that the Prosecutor began disclosing material pursuant to Rule 68 concerning the material from the Hadzihasanovic case. I wanted to remind you that at the Status Conference of the 29th of June, 2005, the Prosecutor accepted in page 42 of the transcript, lines 7 through 11 -- said this, they said they will provide it to the Defence immediately, but until today, we haven't received it. We have had ongoing discussions with the Prosecutor as regards that matter, and we are to raise it yet again today. It is crucial for us and a big problem. I know that a lot of those collections are available on EDS, but I don't believe the Prosecutor has met their obligation pursuant to Rule 68 if they put it on the EDS. First of all, the means Defence has at its disposal and the number of our personnel disallow any such massive search. We have to be realistic to know what any Defence team can do. On the other hand, this Prosecution team was directly involved in this case and they do have current knowledge of what is mitigating material. This is not only material which has been exhibited, be it by Defence or the OTP, but rather during their investigations, they must have come across a lot of material which falls under Rule 68. And I believe Mr. Mundis will be realising it himself and we will discuss this again. I forwarded a large number of criteria to Mr. Mundis, search criteria, but what I'm concerned with is that Mr. Mundis sent a letter in which he stated that some of that material, the material unavailable to us but is in their archives, that that material will be forwarded as late as next spring. The means, the financial resources, given to us by the Registry will expire in December. We will not have the means to deal with it, especially having been given such enormous material as that of yesterday. I truly wanted to ask the Prosecutor - and I'm not saying this to criticise them in any way - I was just asking them to try and understand that they are duty-bound to assist us in preparing our case when it comes to material pursuant to Rule 68 because they have far more means and resources than Defence. I wanted to have this in the transcript. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Vidovic. Comments on these two points, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn very briefly to Annex C of the indictment. Clearly, we have provided the specific information that we have in our possession. With respect to perhaps alternative spellings of names or slight variations in the spellings of names and/or dates or places of birth is the best information we have available or was, I should say, the best information we had available when the indictment was prepared. I will re-visit this issue with my team, and to the extent we can make any corrections to those names, dates, or places of birth, I will notify the Defence accordingly and perhaps seek leave to make a minor amendment to the indictment, to Annex C of the indictment, to correct that information. We will undertake a review of that for certain. With respect to Rule 68, there are a couple of particularly important issues that I also want to put on the record. With respect to the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case, it is clear, as Mrs. Vidovic says, that I was in fact involved in that case, but it is equally clear, as a simple reading of the indictment, a comparative reading of the indictments will show, that there's a huge amount of Rule 68 material that was disclosed in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case that relates to incidents other than the crime base in this case. And our position is that what we're doing is we're reviewing Rule 68 -- reviewing collections for Rule 68 relating to this case, not relating to the Hadzihasanovic and the Kubura case. We should also go to the fact that we don't see a need to disclose Rule 68 material with respect to crimes that are not listed in this indictment. If it goes to the issue of the Mujahedin, it's -- and it's Rule 68, it's disclosed. If it goes to the issue of the murders in Malina and it's Rule 68, it goes to the Defence. If it goes to the issue of Rule 68 in Vares, the Zenica music school, Dusina, Miletici, want and destruction in Grahovici, Brajkovici and other places in Central Bosnia that are not in this indictment, but which were Rule 68 material in the Hadzihasanovic case, that's irrelevant to this proceeding and it's our position that the Defence don't need that material because it has nothing to do with this case. Again, with the exception from Hadzihasanovic and Kubora case of material that relates to the Mujahedin, material that relates to the Malina killings. So it's a bit of apples and oranges to simply say the Hadzihasanovic case, there's some overlap in the indictments between the Delic and Hadzihasanovic cases and, therefore, all the Rule 68 material from Hadzihasanovic must be disclosed in this case. If we're ordered to do that, obviously I'll do it. But we're talking about substantial amounts of information that is not relevant to this case. We're reviewing the material. We're reviewing constantly the in-house material. With respect to actual knowledge, we would be remiss on our end for two reasons if we were not constantly undertaking searches and reviews of material. First of all, and primarily because it's our obligation under Rule 68, which we take very seriously, and second of all, that there might be some material which is relevant to this case which we missed and which might be the subject of a motion in the future to add to an exhibit that we missed. So I assure everyone in this courtroom that we are constantly reviewing this material and as we identify things that are Rule 68, they are disclosed. Let me turn to the issue of the search terms and the ISU search terms. ISU is a unit within OTP that conducts searches. It is true that more than a year ago, Mrs. Vidovic and I met together and came up with a list of terms to be searched. Those terms included place names, names or numerical designators for military units, as well as names of individuals that we both anticipated would feature prominently in this case. Because the case is not docketed, the priority given to those ISU searches by necessity have been a lower priority than cases that are either in trial or that are docketed for trial. Having said that, I have been informed by that unit, that within the next couple of days, I will begin receiving the ISU search results with respect to the accused, Rasim Delic. It is a large number of documents. They will again be reviewed and if there are additional documents which have not already been disclosed and which fall under Rule 68, they will be disclosed. But again, our position has remained consistent, that by making a large number of document collections available in EDS, that the Defence can search that as well, I am clearly aware of my obligation under Rule 68 to disclose material in my actual knowledge. We have done that. We are continuing to do that. It's an ongoing obligation, and we will continue to disclose material in our actual knowledge that falls within the parameters of Rule 68. And I, myself, and my entire team are absolutely committed to continuing to do that. Now, because it's of the ongoing nature of that, we will not be at a point where we can say, Rule 68 disclosure is complete. That's simply not possible. But we are doing everything we can. We have disclosed several hundred documents pursuant to Rule 68. It's my understanding that about 130 to 140 additional Rule 68 documents will be placed in an EDS folder by the end of this month and additional Rule 68 material will be provided when it's identified and when it comes within the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor. Other than that, again, I understand some of the practical difficulties encountered by the Defence, both with respect to EDS in general and in respect of complying with the deadline for filing their pre-trial brief, but the fact of the matter is they have access to EDS and can run searches for certain key terms, places, names, just like we can do. So that would be our general position with respect to Rule 68, and again, it's an issue that I will continue to engage the Defence on, I'm absolutely certain, into the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll be brief. As regards Rule 68, we will address the Bench shortly by way of a motion. I just wanted to ask my colleague to address you regarding our request that has to do with our pre-trial brief, by your leave of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Before we do that, let me just confirm then that regarding the discrepancies in the indictment in Annex C, the Prosecution will undertake a review of that and obviously move for any change in the indictment which this review may call for, and that should be done with expediency. The disclosure of exculpatory material is obviously an important aspect of it, and I understand that the Prosecution is doing what it perceives to be the utmost to satisfy the Defence need in this case. Let me just underscore that when it comes to interpreting the question of relevance, it's obviously for the Prosecution also to take a wide perspective of it and not be restrictive in its interpretation of relevance. It's obviously at this point impossible for the Bench to have any meaning of this, since the material is unknown, but I would like to underscore, that you should take a broad interpretation of what exculpatory the material is. And I also note and, Mrs. Vidovic, with satisfaction that the ISU unit now seems to get its hands or teeth or feet into this material as well which may be of benefit for you. And you anticipated further, Mrs. Vidovic, that you would move on 68 directly. So we'll let this matter then rest for a while. Finally, any issues related to this could also be the subject of a discussion under the auspices of the Senior Legal Officer. So please bear that in mind as well. Now, I'm ready to listen to further submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WHITAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could just deal with the issue of the time-limit for filing our pre-trial brief. Your Honour will appreciate that we've had numerous difficulties in terms of obtaining material from which we start responding to the pre-trial brief. There was a vast amount of material disclosed yesterday which we need to check to ensure that everything said to be disclosed was disclosed. There are a number of translations we're still awaiting for into B/C/S of witness statements and translations of videos that are in Arabic currently, which are said to feature General Delic, of which he doesn't speak Arabic and neither do we, so we require those translations. Your Honour, in relation to those matters that we would seek an extension of the time-limit to file, my learned friend from the Prosecution has already indicated that they accept that a reasonable extension is in order in light of the difficulties we have had. We would ask -- ideally, we would ask for a certain time following full completion of the disclosure obligations and it's not entirely clear when these are going to happen, at least the Arabic translations are not said to be available until next year, I believe, early next year was suggested, but nonetheless, next year. In any event -- and we would be most grateful if the Prosecution could assist in this at all as providing a B/C/S version of the pre-trial brief. We have very, very limited translation facilities at all. I see my learned friend shaking his head. Clearly, this is the central document which requires General Delic to be able to understand. He doesn't speak English, as Your Honour may be aware, to understand it entirely and respond himself. If the Prosecution are unable to assist and the Court are unable to order them to do so, we will have to obviously obtain our own translation. We have very limited monthly translation budget, which again, will delay our capacity to do that. It's in the light of all those matters which we would ask for a time-limit of ideally a month after the Prosecution have completed providing us with all the material so the General can go through the material and the translations provided. In any event, we would ask that this is not before March, in the light of the time -- see, we still await B/C/S versions of statements on which he is to comment. He is to comment on Arabic, on vidoes of which the relevance cannot be understood until they're in a language he understands and indeed that we understand, I understand. And I say if there is no way in which the Prosecution can assist by providing a B/C/S version of the pre-trial brief, that's a further matter which delays us once we've been able to absorb -- firstly, ascertain that it's all there and then absorb all the material that was provided yesterday which in itself -- the checking process is in itself for several weeks of working through a box full of CDs of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Ms. Whitaker. I think I do understand the scope of your predicament. On the other hand, if the Defence pre-trial brief is going to be completed following when every I is dotted and every T is crossed, as far as disclosure is concerned, this could actually take quite some time and I'm a bit reluctant to exceed to that. It seems your position is linked to the lack of resources. I'm not in a position to fully assess those, but I take it you are engaged in a dialogue with the Registry, who are responsible for those matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. WHITAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are, yes. We are still awaiting a response from the 20th of September. It is, of course, with great concern that we view the prospect of -- as Your Honour mentioned, a pre-trial brief light which then becomes substantively reworked during the course of the year because, as it stands, we have no further resources and were to have the prospect of there being an ongoing, rolling, revising of this pre-trial brief which we then are required to respond to with further details is, of course, of great concern. It is with Your Honour's comments, helpful comments, in mind, whereby we would like to ensure our pre-trial brief is the substantive pre-trial brief Defence brief and not a working document which we add and revise as when we ask for the additional time. And it isn't -- it certainly isn't every aspect of disclosure, it is the substantive matter of disclosure on which we require that General Delic to be able to give specific instructions, which we are simply not able to do, particularly with a lack of translation resources of which we have been accorded. But we are hoping that the Registry may be able to assist in our difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Whitaker. Well, the counsel for Mr. Delic is obviously able to communicate with him in a language he understands. I'm not that sympathetic obviously to a notion of a extension, but I cannot -- the time-frame that you have in mind, given the fact that, disregarding for a moment the footnote 1 in the Prosecution pre-trial brief that was filed in time and according to the work-plan. So what I will do at this stage is extend for 14 days your Defence pre-trial brief filing to the 15th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. WHITAKER
utterances.text: Well, could I raise, Your Honour -- it simply won't be possible for us to do that. We simply don't -- we cannot get it into B/C/S in that time-scale. We cannot even check the material that has been disclosed that should have been given to us in accordance with the 31st of October. We can't even check that within that time-scale. We have virtually the resources you see in front of you. They are simply not in a language -- we won't be getting statements in B/C/S on which the General is required to comment by that time and it is not possible for us to, other than leaving huge gaps and saying we will return to this later as and when we are able to, which I submit is the most unsatisfactory. Does the Prosecution except that a reasonable amount of time, and I do believe they were thinking of considerably more than 14 days and certainly beyond the new year, when we would submit, in the light of the other matters, it's not going to be -- this will not cause delay in the long run, but would be of assistance to the Court, we hope, by being of a complete nature. It could only be the most perfunctory document if we were required to submit something by the 15th of December due to the vast quantity of material that we received yesterday and some of it is not in a language which the General understands, particularly, the pre-trial brief. We simply don't have translation facilities to have that done by then. Could I ask whether Your Honour would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mrs. Whitaker, in minded in the light of your repeated entreaties on the matter to give you a further extension on this, but that, I think, is going to be where it rests. And it will also mean that the General and yourself will have to do some work during the holiday season because, which as you know, is prolonged because we have the discrepancy between ours and the Serbs and the original periods. But the Friday of the 20th of January is the time in which you should file your pre-Defence brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. WHITAKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Could I -- when we think of this, have an indication as to the scope of your Defence? I understand that this is a question which is difficult to answer, given the fact what we just have discussed, but some indication I think would be helpful. We know that the Prosecution anticipates to take four months in its case. And with all the caveats that you are rightly entitled to put on an assessment, I still would appreciate if you could give me some indication as to the scope time-wise of your Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. WHITAKER
utterances.text: I think we envisage it would take approximately an equivalent time as the Prosecution, so another four months, very approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As you can understand, we are not here scheduling the details of the case, but I think an indication of the scope would be helpful for those who are doing the planning. With that, we should bring this now, I think, to a close. Fortunately enough, there is no trial following us, otherwise we would be severely punished for exceeding the time-limit. If then the Defence brief is filed and hopefully in a shape, given the limits you have indicated, still would give us a basis to look ahead obviously. There's no point now in speculating as to when the case would go to trial, but if the scheduling part of the Tribunal is so minded, it could very well be in a very brief time after we have completed all the necessary filings and set a date for the -- for the pre-trial conference. I envisage that we should have then a Status Conference sometime in February next year in order to review matters. And to be preceded, hopefully, with the traditional 65 ter conference before that. Now, are there any other issues you want to raise before we adjourn, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you. With that, we are now adjourned.
